notes:
I ran out of searches and page reads before I could get to most of the sites you listed. These notes come from five places: Enduring Word (David Guzik), Gill, Matthew Henry, Constable and Clarke. I also used a few lines from search snippets of The Gospel Coalition's Ezekiel commentary and the 1887 Expositor's Bible. I found nothing from Ellicott, the Pulpit Commentary, Precept Austin's verse notes, any Methodist or Lutheran teachers, modern scholars (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org), Catholic or Orthodox sources, or prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teachers, so those are left out.

**Where the sources split.** The main divide in this chapter is between reading it literally and reading it spiritually:
- **Literal, a future temple age.** Guzik, quoting Feinberg, says the sheer amount of detail is the strongest argument against an allegorical or spiritual reading: "the mass of details and particulars that characterize the last nine chapters of the book. This is the strongest and most irrefutable argument against taking these chapters in an allegorical or symbolical or spiritualizing sense." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-45/)
- **Spiritual, the gospel church.** StudyLight labels John Gill a 1746 Calvinist Baptist (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/45-8.html). He says the chapter is to be understood in a spiritual and evangelic sense, and that its rules differ so much from the law of Moses that they show the old law has been set aside (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-45.html).
- Matthew Henry likewise thinks it seems to point at the new church-state that should be set up under the gospel (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_045.cfm).

---

**v. 1:** Guzik expects a real distribution of land in the time of Ezekiel's temple. Quoting Block, he notes that "you" means the Israelites take part in setting the land aside (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-45/).
- Constable says God would control how the lots fell (Proverbs 16:33). He gives the size as 25,000 cubits long and 10,000 cubits wide (about 8.3 miles by 3.3 miles). The Hebrew text has "rods" rather than "cubits," but long cubits must be the measurement in view (https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-45.html). These sources give the width as 10,000, while the BSB has 20,000; none of them explains why.
- Gill says the passage is not about a literal division of Israel's land. It is mystically and spiritually of the kingdom of Christ. He measures in reeds, which makes the area bigger than all of Canaan, and he takes that as proof that literal Canaan is not meant (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/45-1.html).
- Henry calls the holy portion the "first-fruits" that make the rest holy. He says it was measured so the sanctuary would not slowly take over the whole land (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_045.cfm).
- Clarke reads it as each family settling on its old allotment after the return from exile. He says it is certain that the land was not divided afresh by lot after the Babylonish captivity (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/ezekiel-45.html).

**v. 2:** Constable describes a square about 833 by 833 feet, with a 50-cubit open strip around it like a kind of green belt (https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-45.html).
- Gill reads the square as a picture of how large, complete and stable Christ's church is. He says the open space teaches that we should not rush hastily into the house of God (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-45.html).

**vv. 3–4:** Quoting Vawter and Hoppe, Guzik says the holy district (about 64 square miles) has three strips: one for the Levites, one for the priests that also holds the sanctuary, and one for the city. The prince's land lies to the east and west (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-45/).
- Henry says the priests lived near the sanctuary, unlike in Joshua's day when their towns were spread across the land. He applies this to ministers: gospel ministers should reside upon their charge (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_045.cfm).
- Gill gives two options: the priests' land stands for proper support of gospel ministers, or for all believers as priests to God (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/spa/geb/ezekiel-45.html; this is the Spanish edition of Gill).

**v. 5:** Quoting Wiersbe, Guzik notes that under the old system the Levites were scattered around Israel (Joshua 21). That scattering may also have been a discipline (Genesis 49:5–7) (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-45/).
- Gill takes the Levites' area as a picture of how many members the church will have (Spanish edition, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/spa/geb/ezekiel-45.html).

**v. 6:** Guzik says the city belongs to all Israel, not to any one tribe (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-45/).
- Constable thinks this strip probably lay just to the south and held Jerusalem (https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-45.html).
- Gill sees the city set apart from the holy portion, and connects this with Revelation 21:22 ("I saw no temple therein"). He reads it as church and world kept separate, with Christian rulers governing alike (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/45.htm).

**v. 7:** The Expositor's Bible says the prince's "crown lands" on either side extend to the sea on the west and to the Jordan Valley on the east (https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/n95/ezekiel/44-15.html).
- Gill reads the prince as Christ. Because no size is given for this land, he takes it to show how far Christ's kingdom reaches (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-45.html).
- **Who the prince is** (also relevant to v. 22): Guzik says the prince offers a sin offering and has sons, so he is probably not Jesus (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-44/). He suggests the prince is likely David (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-45/).

**v. 8:** Quoting Feinberg, Guzik points to Ahab taking Naboth's vineyard (1 Kings 21) as the kind of seizure that will no longer happen (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-45/).
- Henry says the prince is given plenty so he won't be tempted to oppress. He adds that only God's grace actually prevents it (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_045.cfm).
- Gill reads "the house of Israel" as the spiritual Israel of Jews and Gentiles (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/45-8.html).
- The Gospel Coalition commentary sets the prince's just rule against Israel's earlier leaders. It says the new prince will set the example socially. Religiously, he retains a mission-critical role. (https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/ezekiel/)

**v. 9:** Guzik says this picture of future justice was meant to stir Ezekiel's own leaders to change (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-45/).
- Henry says a long habit of wrongdoing never makes it acceptable: no prescription will justify a wrong (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_045.cfm).
- Gill applies it to Christian rulers: no crushing taxes, unfair lawsuits or unjust verdicts (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/45.htm).

**vv. 10–12:** Guzik says God cares about plain honesty in trade. Quoting Feinberg, he explains the units: the ephah (about a bushel, dry), the bath (about nine gallons, liquid), and the hin (a sixth of a bath) (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-45/).
- Gill points to Amos 8:5 on cheating with measures and says the ephah was for dry goods and the bath for liquids. He warns not to confuse the homer with the much smaller "omer" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/45.htm).

**vv. 13–15:** Quoting Vawter and Hoppe, Guzik says the people share responsibility for supporting public worship. On "to make atonement," he quotes Alexander: these rites look back to Christ's finished work and were in no way efficacious. They were picture-lessons and reminders (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-45/).
- Gill says the offering is for the upkeep of ministers of the gospel, not for a temple dedication as the Jewish commentator Kimchi thought (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/45.htm).
- Henry says we honour God by giving Him His due from whatever we have, though God needs nothing from us (Psalm 50:9) (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_045.cfm).

**vv. 16–17:** Guzik says the prince collects the people's gifts so he can offer them to the LORD on their behalf (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-45/).
- Gill reads the prince providing the offerings as Christ, whose obedience, suffering and death fulfilled the law and atoned for sin (Spanish edition, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/spa/geb/ezekiel-45.html).

**vv. 18–19:** Clarke, quoted by Guzik, says "There is nothing of this in the Mosaic law; it seems to have been a new ceremony. An annual purification of the sanctuary may be intended." Wright, also quoted, says the temple needs cleansing because its ministers are human and sinful (Hebrews 9:23) (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-45/).
- Henry says worshippers should renew their repentance together and apply Christ's blood, and that the start of the year is a good time for it, as Hezekiah did (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_045.cfm).

**v. 20:** Guzik quotes Alexander that this future age has no special Day of Atonement, because the cross fulfilled it. He also quotes F. B. Meyer: the "erring and simple" were remembered in this offering, and we should remember them when we pray (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-45/).
- Henry says these are sins of ignorance or oversight, whether by priests, Levites or people (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_045.cfm).

**v. 21:** Guzik says Passover will keep both the Exodus and Christ's cross in memory (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-45/). He also notes these chapters mention Passover, Tabernacles and Firstfruits but not Pentecost (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-40/).
- Henry connects it to Christ our passover (1 Corinthians 5:7). He calls the Lord's Supper "our passover-feast" and says the whole Christian life is a feast of unleavened bread (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_045.cfm).

**v. 22:** Guzik's point that the prince needs a sin offering, and so is probably not the Messiah, applies here (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-44/).

**vv. 23–25:** Henry says the constant repetition shows the old sacrifices fell short, because they could not make the comers thereunto perfect (Hebrews 10:1). Christ's atonement was offered once for all, but the sacrifices of a broken and thankful heart should be offered daily (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_045.cfm).
- Guzik's chapter ends without saying anything specific about v. 25 (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-45/). On the next chapter, he says the daily offerings of this future age look back to Christ rather than forward (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-46/).
